items.q: What is the difference between a transformation and an action?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Transformations (filter, select, groupBy, join) are lazy -- they build a DAG of operations. Actions (show, collect, count, write) trigger actual execution -- Spark optimizes the full DAG and submits tasks. Laziness enables optimization: Spark can push filters down and choose join strategies across the entire plan before executing anything.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

items.q: What is a shuffle and why is it expensive?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A shuffle redistributes data across partitions so matching keys end up on the same executor. Occurs during groupBy, join, repartition. Requires intermediate files on disk and network transfer between nodes. The shuffle is the primary optimization target -- reduce its size (filter before groupBy), eliminate it (broadcast small tables).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

items.q: Why write Parquet instead of CSV?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Parquet is columnar -- analytical queries reading only a few columns read only those from disk. CSV reads entire rows. Parquet also compresses effectively, stores schema (no type inference needed), and supports partition pruning. Typically 10-100x faster to read than CSV for analytics queries.

items.q: What is a broadcast join and when should you use it?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A broadcast join copies the smaller table to every executor -- the large table never moves. Eliminates the shuffle on the large table, typically 5-20x speedup. Use broadcast() explicitly for tables Spark does not auto-broadcast (above 10MB but below ~100MB). Check explain() to confirm BroadcastHashJoin appears in the plan.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server compiles T-SQL into an execution plan based on statistics histogram estimates. Parameter sniffing occurs when a plan compiled for a specific parameter (e.g. 1 row) is reused for a parameter matching 1,000,000 rows, leading to index scan or memory grant spills.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Implicit datatype conversion (e.g. passing NVARCHAR parameter to VARCHAR indexed column) forces SQL Server to run CONVERT() on every row, turning index seeks into full index scans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) eliminates reader-writer blocking using tempdb row versioning, but increases tempdb I/O and version store management overhead.

items.q: When should you cache a Spark DataFrame?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Cache when the same DataFrame is used in MORE than one action in the same job AND upstream transformations are expensive (multiple joins, UDFs). Do not cache when used only once, too large for executor memory, or when the source is fast to read.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Boxing inside a high-throughput loop generates thousands of ephemeral Gen 0 objects, triggering frequent GC pauses and thread pool delays. Fix: use generic collection interfaces (IList<T>) and Span<T>/Memory<T> for byte slicing.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).

items.q: Why is checkpointing mandatory in Structured Streaming?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The checkpoint directory records the stream offset (how far the job has processed) and aggregation state. On crash and restart, Spark reads the checkpoint and resumes exactly where it stopped -- not reprocessing everything. Without checkpointing, a restart reprocesses all data or loses progress.

items.q: How does Spark AQE dynamically convert a SortMergeJoin to a BroadcastHashJoin at runtime?
items.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** During initial shuffle stage execution, AQE measures actual materialized output partition sizes. If one side of the join is smaller than spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, Spark dynamically changes the physical execution plan from SortMergeJoin to BroadcastHashJoin without re-running the query.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

AQE detects partition size imbalance, splits the heavy skewed partition into smaller sub-partitions, and replicates matching keys from the join target.
